A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same interference-aware graph-coloring scheduler, renamed SON-GOKU in v4. Their main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures support comparison, including matching material relocated between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments across six benchmarks, including optimizer combinations and two scheduler ablations (Table 2).

after.justification: v4 retains those experiments and adds original Taskonomy evaluations, runtime and memory measurements, additional ablations and training-dynamics analyses.

M1.justification: The core EMA, conflict graph, greedy coloring and cyclic update procedure remains. v4 restricts minimum-frequency task duplication to compatible slots (Section 4.4.1) and adds a tested TAG lookahead-affinity alternative to cosine scoring (Appendix P). Sketching options already appeared in v1 Appendix G.5.

E1.justification: The original six benchmarks and auxiliary-task definitions are retained. v4 adds Taskonomy, including its Tiny subset, covering Euclidean and Z-buffer depth, occlusion and texture edges, keypoints, normals, curvature and reshading. This substantially expands evaluation on naturally occurring visual prediction tasks.

E2.justification: The nine standalone comparison methods in v1 Table 2 remain in v4 Table 1. Additional comparisons include graph-construction variants, SON-GOKU with TAG affinities, and a no-refresh timing control (Tables 1, 8–9). TAG is evaluated as an affinity replacement within the scheduler, not as a standalone grouping baseline.

E3.justification: The original benchmark settings are largely retained. New protocols include density-matched graph controls, synthetic timing workloads with 1024-dimensional gradients over 900 steps and varying task counts/refresh periods, and Taskonomy encoder-width and refresh-period sweeps (Appendices K, L and R). These are added evaluation designs rather than established reruns under changed original settings.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained static-coloring and single-step-history ablations, v4 tests alternative edge rules and density matching, approximation speed–accuracy tradeoffs, TAG affinities, and sensitivity to backbone width and refresh period. Appendix S adds task-group, conflict-density, convergence and graph-evolution analyses absent from v1.

E5.justification: v1 reports benchmark point estimates without empirical repeat counts. v4 adds ± values to retained results, standard deviations and repeated trials for timing/memory studies, two seeds for TAG evaluation, and percentile bands for graph statistics. Table 1 does not define its ± convention or run count; the PDFs do not establish increased replication of the original experiments.

E6.justification: Most original benchmark means remain unchanged. NYUv2 mIoU changes from 0.63 to 0.063 for MGDA, 0.65 to 0.065 for CAGrad, 0.69 to 0.069 for AdaTask, and 0.68 to 0.068 for scheduler AdaTask. v4 adds extensive ablation, Taskonomy, timing, memory and scaling results. For example, Table 8 newly reports depth RMSE of 18.6199 for cosine affinities versus 18.3034 for TAG; this is not a cross-version performance gain.

T1.justification: v4 replaces the incorrect 1 - tau gradient-energy factor with 1 - tau(|S| - 1), introduces an aggregate conflict ratio, and substantially rewrites the convergence analysis. It also corrects EMA effective-sample-size calculations and randomized-class gradient scaling, and adds affinity and signal-to-noise derivations. Much of v1's graph-recovery and scheduled-versus-aggregated analysis is retained in renamed Appendices B–C.

C1.justification: Despite renaming and rewriting, the principal contribution claims remain interference-aware graph-color scheduling, compatibility with existing optimizers, theoretical guarantees, gains across six main benchmarks, and the importance of recoloring and historical averaging. The expanded appendix evidence mainly elaborates and supports these retained claims.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive interpretations of backbone-dependent benefits, refresh frequency versus noise/staleness, training-time grouping behavior, and TAG/sketching performance–cost tradeoffs. It qualifies gradient-energy guarantees by group size and discusses affinity-specific recovery limitations. Section 7.3.3 additionally extrapolates to generalization under distribution shift without adding a dedicated shift evaluation.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-access link and reproducibility statement describing preprocessing and configured training scripts. It also expands pseudocode and documents new experimental details, including synthetic timing procedures, sketch widths, the 0.1 TAG probe step, and three-epoch, batch-size-64 Taskonomy training. Repository contents cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands positioning against task-grouping approaches and presents the scheduler as compatible with alternative affinity estimators. Appendices P–R develop connections to clustered learning, gradient signal-to-noise and model capacity, adding works such as Jacob et al. (2008) and Michalkiewicz et al. (2023). Much earlier related work is retained in Appendix M.

P1.justification: The introduction and theoretical overview are extensively rewritten. Detailed related work, dataset descriptions and comparator descriptions move into appendices, existing proofs are reordered, and a reproducibility section is added. The title and author block change, and SON-GOKU replaces the generic scheduler terminology throughout.

P2.justification: The original pipeline figure is retained, while the performance table gains uncertainty entries and ablation rows and the dataset table moves to Appendix J. v4 adds numerous runtime, memory and Taskonomy tables, scaling plots, convergence curves and graph snapshots, and reformats the algorithm as numbered pseudocode. Table 11 redisplays the cosine results already in Table 8.

improvement.justification: v4 corrects v1's group-size bound and adds useful controls, uncertainty reporting, Taskonomy evidence and reproducibility information. However, important inconsistencies remain: Section 5.2 attributes a tau-dependent convergence penalty that Appendix F no longer supports, Appendices D and N give unreconciled persistent-memory descriptions, and Figure 6(o) plots negative MSE without explanation. These affect central theoretical and efficiency claims and the credibility of new analyses. The benefits and reliability problems do not support a confident net quality judgment.
